title: Sales, stock and credit: know what you sold and who owes you

say: Sales, stock and credit: know what you sold, and who owes you.
This is the video for Module 2, Sales, stock and credit records.
Your sales book is the most used page in your business. If you only keep one record, keep this one.

panel.heading: Three records that protect your money
items: Sales book: every sale, and how it was paid
Stock card: what came in, went out, is left
Debtors list: who owes you, and when

say: Your stock card shows where most of your business money is sitting: on the shelves.

say: And your debtors list gets your money back. Credit keeps customers loyal, but it is the fastest way for a small business to run out of money.

panel.heading: Three records that protect your money
items: Sales book: every sale, and how it was paid

Debtors list: who owes you, and when

say: Each sale gets one line: date, item, quantity, price, total, and how it was paid. Cash, transfer, or credit.
For example, Funke sells foodstuff in Ibadan.

She sells 4 paint buckets of garri at about 3,500 naira for cash, that is 14,000 naira. She also tallies 12 small cups of crayfish at about 500 naira, another 6,000 naira. Her cash sales are 20,000 naira.
Two buckets of beans at about 5,000 naira are paid by transfer. That is 10,000 naira.
And one bottle of palm oil goes to Iya Sade on credit, 2,500 naira.
All sales come to about 32,500 naira. Now she knows exactly what to check: 20,000 more cash in her purse, 10,000 more in her account, and Iya Sade in her debtors list.
At closing, step one. Add the Total column for the whole day.

panel.heading: Check your sales book
items: Add the Total column for the day
Count cash, minus the float
Tick transfers against your bank app
Check every credit sale is in the debtors list
Write any difference with a note

say: Step two. Count your cash and take away the float, the change money you started with. The rest should equal your cash sales.

panel.heading: Check your sales book
items: Add the Total column for the day
Count cash, minus the float
Tick transfers against your bank app
Check every credit sale is in the debtors list
Write any difference with a note

say: Step three. Open your bank or wallet app and tick each incoming transfer against a line in your book. Unmatched alerts often mean a forgotten sale.
Always confirm the money is in your own account before goods leave. Never trust only the customer's phone screen.

panel.heading: Check your sales book
items: Add the Total column for the day
Count cash, minus the float
Tick transfers against your bank app
Check every credit sale is in the debtors list
Write any difference with a note
panel.rule: Confirm the transfer in your own account before releasing goods.

say: Step four, check every credit sale is in your debtors list. And step five, write any difference with a short note. Short now and then is normal. Short almost every day means something is wrong.

panel.heading: Check your sales book
items: Add the Total column for the day
Count cash, minus the float
Tick transfers against your bank app
Check every credit sale is in the debtors list
Write any difference with a note
panel.rule: Confirm the transfer in your own account before releasing goods.

say: Opening stock, plus stock bought, minus stock sold, equals what should be left. Count what is really left and compare.
For example, Esther sells soft drinks by the crate in Port Harcourt. On Monday she counts 10 crates.

panel.heading: The stock formula
items: Opening stock: 10 crates
Plus bought: 15 crates
Minus closing count: 7 crates
18 crates left the shop
Sales book shows 17: 1 crate missing

say: She buys 15 more on Wednesday, so 25 crates were available.

panel.heading: The stock formula
items: Opening stock: 10 crates
Plus bought: 15 crates
Minus closing count: 7 crates
18 crates left the shop
Sales book shows 17: 1 crate missing

say: On Saturday she counts 7 crates. So 18 crates left the shop.

panel.heading: The stock formula
items: Opening stock: 10 crates
Plus bought: 15 crates
Minus closing count: 7 crates
18 crates left the shop
Sales book shows 17: 1 crate missing

say: But her sales book shows only 17 sold. One crate, about 6,000 naira at cost, is unexplained.
Her helper explains: 2 bottles broke and some were given to visitors. Now Esther writes breakages and gifts in the Out column, and the gap disappears.

panel.heading: The stock formula
items: Opening stock: 10 crates
Plus bought: 15 crates
Minus closing count: 7 crates
18 crates left the shop
Sales book shows 17: 1 crate missing

say: Count at the same time each week, for example Saturday after closing. Write breakages, spoilage and goods taken for home in the Out column. Sell older stock first.
And never sell food, drinks or medicines past their expiry date. Remove them, record them as spoiled, and buy smaller quantities next time.

panel.heading: When you count your stock
items: Same day and time each week
Record breakages and home use as Out
Sell older stock first
Never sell expired food, drinks or medicine

say: Write every debt in front of the customer and read it back with the due date. Record each part payment and the new balance.
For example, Chioma sells fabric in Aba. At month end, Ada, Joy and Uche owe her 73,000 naira. Uche's debt is 7 weeks old.
Next week's stock will cost about 120,000 naira, and she has only 60,000 in hand. So she calls Ada today, agrees a date with Joy, and stops credit to Uche.
Sort debts by age and chase the oldest first. The longer a debt waits, the harder it is to collect.
Set your rules. Credit only for regular customers you know, a limit per person, a clear payment date, no new credit until the last debt is paid, and no credit sale without a line in the list.

panel.heading: Set your credit rules
items: Who: regular customers with a working phone
How much: a limit per person
How long: a clear payment date
One at a time: no new credit until paid
Write it every time
